sentences.t: The booth was at the Denny's on the corner of Capitol and Berryessa in East San Jose, chosen because Jensen Huang had once washed dishes, bused tables and waited tables at Denny's - "Denny's I consider it my first company", he says.

Through late 1992 and into 1993 he met Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem there, two Sun Microsystems engineers he knew from his own days at LSI Logic, where he had been the engineer assigned to their graphics project.

The three would order one bottomless cup of coffee each and work for four hours, Malachowsky recalls, until they ran out of things to talk about; then they would go home and come back and do it again (Sequoia's Crucible Moments).
What they settled on was unfashionable twice over.
The PC revolution was beginning, and they reasoned the one thing a home computer would do more than anything in the world was play games - which meant 3D graphics, a market measured at zero.

"If you were to go to market research firms and you asked them, well, what's the market size for 3D graphics for PCs in 1993, the answer would've been zero", says Mark Stevens, the Sequoia partner who joined the board in 1993 and remains on it today.
Gaming carried no respect: the market was small, and its players were teenagers.
None of the three had even seen a PC before; they bought a Gateway 2000 and tore it apart to learn the industry they were about to enter.
Huang's first day of work was February 17, 1993 - his birthday.

His old boss at LSI Logic, Wilfred Corrigan, picked up the phone and called Don Valentine: I'm going to send a kid your way, he's one of my best employees, I'm not sure what he's going to do, but give him money.
Huang, 29, pitched badly.
Valentine funded him anyway, with one parting sentence: "If you lose my money, I'll kill you".
The company was incorporated in California that April (the episode; Nvidia's investor FAQ).
The first chip took 18 to 24 months and came out as everything at once.

The NV1 combined 3D graphics, video processing, audio wave-table processing, an IO port, a game port and its own programming model - with dongles spilling out of the box and almost no applications to run on it.
Huang's verdict is the autopsy in one sentence: "It was a great technology achievement.
It was a terrible product".
Stevens calls it a Swiss Army knife, overpriced for a market that wanted one thing - a fast, cheap 3D chip.
The launch customer, Diamond Multimedia, took 250,000 units.
Retail sales failed, Diamond panicked, and 249,000 came back.
"250,000 units went out.
250,000, well, 249,000 came back", Huang says.
It practically put the company out of business (the episode).
Worse, the architecture underneath was wrong.

The NV1 and its in-development successor, the NV2, rendered in quadrangles; in 1995 Microsoft shipped Windows 95 with DirectX, and the rest of the industry - by then some 50 competitors - standardized on triangles.
The NV2 existed because of a lifeline: Sega, whose Virtua Fighter and Daytona arcade games were revolutionary, had contracted Nvidia to build its next console.
Finishing it meant two more years building the wrong architecture.
Not finishing it meant the money stopped.
"I was confronted with a situation where we would finish the project and die, or not finish the project and die right away" (the episode).
So Huang went to Sega's CEO, Irimajiri-san, with an ask no one is entitled to make: release Nvidia from the console contract, and pay the contract in full anyway.

The argument was honesty itself - if we finish this console for you, our company goes out of business, and the architecture we would build you is the wrong one, because the world is moving to inverse texture mapping.
Irimajiri thought about it for a couple of days and came back: I'd like to help you.
Sega paid out the remaining roughly $5 million and got nothing for it.
"You can't discount the kindness of people", Huang says of that moment.
It was all the money the company had, and it bought just enough time to hunker down (the episode).
These were the years behind Huang's most repeated sentence at Nvidia: "We're only 30 days away from going out of business".
Stevens confirms it was not a slogan.

In the mid-nineties, on a few occasions, it was arithmetic: the company was burning cash on some of the most expensive silicon engineers in Silicon Valley, competing for talent with Silicon Graphics and Apple, and the investors were openly worried about whether Nvidia would ever reach escape velocity (the episode).
The last chip had to work the first time.
Conventional chip design ran tapeout, bring-up, debug, re-tapeout - a year to eighteen months of iterations Nvidia did not have.
Huang's reasoning inverted it: "If we need more than one tapeout, we don't need it.
We'll be out of business".
The answer was to finish everything in software before silicon existed - six to eight months of work on complete fumes.
When a company called Icos went out of business, Huang heard it had an in-circuit emulator sitting in a warehouse, a refrigerator-sized machine that lets a PC pretend the final chip already exists.
Nvidia bought the scraps.
The RIVA 128 - internally NV3 - became, in Huang's telling, the first PC chip the world ever emulated.
It taped out, and it worked the first time (the episode).
The RIVA 128 sold a million units in its first four months and saved the company.

The deeper dividend was the process: the emulation-first method let Nvidia ship new chips at more than twice the cadence of competitors, and the survivors of the 50-company 3D shakeout thinned quickly from there.
The company that had been waiting on Stevens's surfboard for the market wave finally felt it come in (the episode).
The fifth chip changed the noun.
The GeForce 256, in late 1999, added programmability to acceleration - "the world's first programmable accelerator", as Huang calls it: the world's first GPU, and the first programmable accelerator.
The programmability let game developers write shaders, and creativity in games exploded.
The same year, the company went public: January 22, 1999, at $12 a share, reincorporated in Delaware the year before.
In a twist, Microsoft - whose DirectX had nearly rendered Nvidia extinct - picked GeForce to power the original Xbox (the episode; Nvidia's investor FAQ).
By the mid-2000s the company was successful, public, and boxed in: the PC market's growth was asymptoting, and Nvidia's lane meant knocking heads with Intel forever.
The escape hatch was the programmability itself.
In 2006 the company released CUDA, a general-purpose programming layer for its GPUs, and then watched where it drifted.
Graduate students were buying GeForce cards at electronics stores to run research simulations.

A quantum chemist in Taiwan invited Huang to National Taiwan University, opened a closet, and showed him an array of GeForce cards on shelves with house fans strapped on: "I built my own personal supercomputer" - and told him that because of Nvidia's work, he could do his own work within his lifetime (the episode).

At Stanford, Andrew Ng's group reached the same idea from the other side: around 2008-2009 his students - including Ian Goodfellow, who built the lab's first GPU server in a dorm room - found that neural networks trained 10 to 100 times faster on GPUs, doing thousands of things in parallel instead of one step after another.
Hinton's lab in Toronto and LeCun's at NYU were doing the same.
Then came AlexNet, the 2012 image-recognition breakthrough, and the signal was unmistakable to anyone watching.
The market for AI chips, Stevens points out, was exactly as large as the 3D-graphics market had been in 1993: zero billion dollars.
AI had stalled and restarted for forty years; spending R&D on it was betting the company on a market that might never exist.
Nvidia did it anyway - a wholesale pivot, in Huang's words, that pulled cost, people and attention away from the core business.
The company sought out every serious AI researcher on the planet and treated each small adoption as the positive reinforcement a long bet needs (the episode).
The bet resolved a decade later, in five days.

When ChatGPT launched in November 2022 it reached a million users in five days and 100 million in eight weeks - the fastest adoption of a technology product ever recorded - and the compute underneath it was Nvidia's.

Huang's framing of the new physics: where Moore's Law advanced computing about 10 times every five years, the AI era compounds at the chip, system, algorithm and model layers at once - "a million times every ten years", a pace the industry has taken to calling Huang's Law.
The company that had been told for years it was "just gaming" had become, by the time Sequoia told this story, the third most valuable company in the world (the episode).
Which is the company the SEC is now examining.

On Friday, Reuters reported that enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at Nvidia - which issues, opened when, whether they become a case, all unknown; the SEC declined comment and Nvidia did not respond.
The stock closed the week at $125.53, down 13.8% on the day and 23% on the week - the sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, 46% off the peak.
On Tuesday's earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said the company is proud of supporting the AI industry and "would be far more selective moving forward" about AI financing deals.

The scene to hold is the symmetry, not the verdict: a company that has twice stood weeks from death over accounting of a different kind - cash in, cash out, one tapeout - now answers questions about what its record revenues are made of.
Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing, and many close without action; what the filings say next is the story.
The founders' own summary of the first thirty years is Malachowsky's: "It feels like this overnight success was 30 years in the making" (Reuters; CNBC; The Verge).
